Every evening at his father's hardware shop in Gadag, between customers, Lokesh watched the Swamiji videos on his phone. The man spoke so calmly about purpose and discipline that Lokesh felt, for the first time, that his life had a shape.

He started waking early, sweeping the shop before school without being asked. His father noticed and smiled.

Madhav, his friend from the bus, sat on the shop step one evening and asked, "Is he the one who says phones are poison? While being on your phone?"

Lokesh laughed. "He says a lot of things."

That night, though, he wrote them down. Wake early, be honest, respect parents: good. Tell ten people. Donate to the ashram before full moon. Don't read other teachers, they'll confuse you.

The last one bothered him. The next day he borrowed a book on the Gita from the school library and asked his Kannada teacher what she thought. He kept the early mornings. He stopped at the donation part.

qa.q: Where did Lokesh watch the videos?
qa.a: Lokesh watched them at his father's hardware shop in Gadag.

qa.q: What did Lokesh feel while watching the Swamiji videos?
qa.a: Lokesh felt inspired and calm, as if his life finally had a shape and purpose.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that was wise?
qa.a: Lokesh wrote down what the speaker asked, noticed the warning sign of not reading other teachers, and checked with a library book and his teacher while keeping the good habits.

By March, Wanjiru had watched every sermon the online pastor had posted. He had an answer for everything, and she started to feel sorry for everyone who didn't listen.

At lunch in her Nairobi school she caught herself thinking her friend Xin, who didn't go to any church, was simply lost. When Xin talked about her weekend, Wanjiru barely listened.

Then, in Tuesday's sermon, the pastor said that a famous scientist had "admitted on his deathbed that evolution was a lie." Wanjiru repeated it to Xin, proudly.

Xin frowned. "Where's that from? Can we check?"

They checked in the library. The story had been made up decades ago; the scientist's family had denied it.

Wanjiru felt hot with embarrassment. She realised she'd stopped checking anything he said. She'd stopped listening to anyone else.

That evening she didn't open the app. She asked Xin to come to the drama club with her, and she started a list: claims to check.

qa.q: Where did Wanjiru and Xin check the pastor's story?
qa.a: They checked in the library.

qa.q: What was Wanjiru feeling when the story turned out to be made up?
qa.a: Wanjiru felt embarrassed, hot-faced, and shaken to realise she had stopped checking anything the pastor said.

qa.q: What steps did Wanjiru take after that, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Wanjiru took a break from the app, invited Xin to drama club and started a list of claims to check, which keeps her curious and connected to different people.

qa.q: How might Xin have felt when Wanjiru barely listened at lunch?
qa.a: Xin may have felt hurt and pushed aside, as if Wanjiru saw her as less worth listening to.

In the boys' hostel of the Jaipur school, Mridul had become known as "the preacher's boy." He played the videos loudly at night and told his roommates they were wasting their lives on cricket and films. "You're all lost. He's the only one telling the truth."

Kamal, the senior monitor of their floor, sat on the edge of Mridul's bed one evening. "Can I ask you something? Not to fight."

"Okay."

"When did you last disagree with him about anything?"

Mridul opened his mouth, then shut it. He couldn't remember.

"He said last week that eating after sunset makes you weak," Kamal said. "Did you check that?"

"No."

"Check one thing. Just one. With your biology sir or the library."

Mridul did. The claim wasn't true. He felt foolish, then oddly relieved. On Friday he went back to the cricket nets with his roommates and apologised for calling them lost. He still watched some videos. But now he kept a notebook of what to check.

qa.a: Mridul was known as "the preacher's boy."

"Saving my pocket money. For the mission."

"The guy in the videos?"

Karthik lowered his voice. "He says my family is spiritually asleep. That's why I feel so bad at home. If I give an offering and keep it between me and him, I'll be free. He sends me messages at night."

Sahil stopped in the hallway. "He's messaging you? And telling you to keep secrets from your family?"

"He said they wouldn't understand."

Looking back, the scariest thing is how normal it felt. I'm Joseph, and in Class 9 I found a preacher's channel that seemed to explain why I felt so alone. He said most people, even families, were "blind." Only his followers could see.

Then came the private group. Every night he posted things like, "If your family mocks your faith, they are not your real family." He asked for "seed offerings." He said, "What we share here stays here."

I sent him my birthday money. I stopped eating dinner with my parents because he said they would pull me down. I felt guilty all the time, guilty at home, guilty in the group.

My elder sister Jaya noticed I'd stopped laughing. She found me crying on the stairs and asked, very gently, what was going on. I showed her the group.

She sat with me, then took me straight to our mother. Amma read it all that evening, held my hand and said, "None of this is your fault." We reported the group together that night.

qa.q: What did the preacher call the money he asked for?
qa.a: He called them "seed offerings."

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling during the months in the group?
qa.a: Joseph felt lonely and constantly guilty, both at home and in the group.

qa.q: What warning signs of manipulation are in the preacher's messages?
qa.a: He asked for money, demanded secrecy, and told Joseph the family at home was not a real family, which isolates and controls someone.

qa.q: How did Jaya help Joseph, and why did that matter?
qa.a: Jaya noticed Joseph had stopped laughing, asked gently and took Joseph to their mother that evening, so a trusted adult could step in the same day.

grounding: It shows a teen targeted by a preacher who uses guilt and us-versus-them to get money and cut off family, recognising it and telling a trusted adult.

For a year, Thabo had watched every video by the pastor from Pretoria who preached simple living. "Wealth is a trap," he said, in a plain white shirt. Thabo gave away his old sneakers to a younger boy because of him.

Then, in the school library in Johannesburg, his friend Emil pushed his phone across the table. An article. Photos of the pastor's three luxury cars, his mansion, and a new "Prosperity Pack" his followers could buy.

Thabo stared. His face went hot. "I defended him. At my uncle's braai. I told everyone he was different."

"You weren't stupid," Emil said. "He was good at it."

Thabo walked home angry, at the pastor and at himself. That night he sat on his bed and wrote two lists. What he'd been told that was true: be generous, don't chase things, help younger kids. What was a lie: the man.

He unfollowed the channel. He kept the first list taped inside his cupboard.

He turned the monitor towards her. A news report: the online scholar he had followed for two years, the one who preached humility and poverty, had been found with a luxury flat abroad and a donation scheme that paid him directly.

I still cringe about the student council debate last year. I'm Anand, and I'd been campaigning for weeks for the climate club's plan to ban plastic in the canteen.

In the Q and A, Nandini raised her hand and said, smirking, "So we'll all eat off banana leaves because Anand watched one documentary?" A few people laughed.

My face went hot. I had an insult ready, something about her family's plastics shop. I actually opened my mouth.

Then I stopped. I counted to three, like our debate coach told us. And I asked, "What do you mean? Is it the cost you're worried about?"

She looked surprised. "Yeah, actually. The steel plates are more expensive, and the canteen uncle already struggles."

That was a real point. I hadn't thought about it.

We ended up working out a slow switch together. I still think plastic is a problem. But I learned that Nandini wasn't the enemy. She just saw a different cost.

Social science teacher's note, Class 11 mock election, Thursday

During the mock election debate today, Shreya mocked the candidate Sumit's group was supporting. "Their leader couldn't organise a tiffin box, let alone a school." The room laughed. I watched Sumit's hands clench on the desk and his face go red. He stood up fast.

I expected an insult. We have had trolling in the class chat group before.

Instead, he stood for a moment without speaking. Then he said, tightly, "Okay. What exactly do you think he'd do badly?" Shreya was caught off guard and gave two real points about the budget plan. Sumit wrote them down and answered one of them.

Afterwards I spoke to him. He said, "I wanted to say something awful about her. Then I remembered she helped me with chemistry all last year. She's not her opinion."

I praised the pause. I will use this in next week's lesson on disagreement, without names.

qa.q: What did Shreya say about the leader?
qa.a: Shreya said, "Their leader couldn't organise a tiffin box, let alone a school."

qa.a: It suggests Sumit felt a flash of anger at the mockery and wanted to hit back.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Pausing and asking what exactly she thought the leader would do badly worked, because it turned mockery into real points he could answer.

qa.q: How might Shreya see Sumit's reply?
qa.a: Shreya was caught off guard, perhaps expecting an insult, and may respect him more for taking her points seriously.

On the tram home, Siddiq realised he'd been picturing a cartoon, not a person. Beatriz wasn't stupid or evil. She was scared about the same thing he was, from a different angle.

But he noticed he ate lunch with fewer people every week. And Gautam, who had argued the opposite side in the last round, just stopped talking to him.

One Friday the teacher paired them for the regional competition, arguing the same motion. Sachin groaned.

That evening Sachin deleted his joke from the club chat. He still disagreed with Gautam on most of it. But he started saying, "I think," before his opinions again.

I'll tell you what happened, since you asked for the school safety talk. I'm Parul. Last year I posted a short video for our social science project about why our town should keep a common prayer ground open to everyone.

Within an hour, the comments turned. Strangers. Some attacked my opinion, which was fine. Then they attacked my religion. Names I won't repeat. One said, "People like you should leave." My hands were shaking so much I dropped my phone.

I wanted to reply. I'd even typed something nasty back. I deleted it.

Instead I did what Usha ma'am had told us in class: I screenshotted everything, blocked the worst accounts and turned off comments. Then I went to school early and showed her the screenshots.

She read them with me. She said, "Disagreeing with you is allowed. This isn't." She called my parents and reported the accounts with the school's cyber safety team that same morning.

I still feel the sting. But I didn't become like them.

qa.q: What did one comment say to Parul?
qa.a: One comment said, "People like you should leave."

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when the comments turned to religion?
qa.a: Parul felt frightened and hurt, with hands shaking so much the phone fell.

qa.q: Which steps did Parul take that were wise?
qa.a: Parul did not reply in kind, took screenshots, blocked the worst accounts, turned off comments and told Usha ma'am the next morning.

qa.q: How does Usha ma'am see the comments?
qa.a: Usha ma'am sees a clear line: disagreeing with Parul is allowed, but cruelty about religion is not, so she acts that same morning.

grounding: It shows a teen abused online for an opinion and religion who does not reply in kind, blocks, saves proof, tells a trusted adult and learns that disagreement is not permission for cruelty.

Sunday. Kalyani posted in the city's youth forum that the new flyover would cut through the old market and hurt small shopkeepers. By night, her phone was full. Some people disagreed politely. Others didn't. "Go back to school, stupid girl." "Traitor to development." Someone found her photo and posted it with insults. She sat up till two, typing and deleting angry replies.

Monday. Dolma found her in the library, grey-faced. "Don't answer them," Dolma said. "Screenshot everything. Every name, every time." They did it together, then blocked eleven accounts. After school Kalyani showed her father. He went quiet, then said, "You had every right to your opinion. They have no right to this." He reported the accounts that evening and emailed the forum moderators.

Thursday. Two accounts had been removed. The photo post was gone. Kalyani still felt shaky when her phone buzzed. But she hadn't sent a single reply. She wrote a new post about the market, calmer, with facts, and turned comments off.

qa.q: How many accounts did Kalyani and Dolma block?
qa.a: They blocked eleven accounts.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling on Sunday night?
qa.a: Kalyani felt hurt, angry and frightened, sitting up till two typing and deleting angry replies.

qa.q: What steps helped Kalyani, and why?
qa.a: Not replying, saving screenshots, blocking and telling her father helped, because it kept proof and let a trusted adult report the abuse.

qa.q: How does Kalyani's father see what happened?
qa.a: He sees her opinion as her right and the abuse as unacceptable, and acts that same evening by reporting it.

grounding: It shows a teen abused online for her opinion who does not reply in kind, blocks, saves proof and tells a trusted adult, learning that disagreement is not permission for cruelty.
